DISTROS.name: Debian
DISTROS.best: People who value calm over newness. Debian powers half the servers you will ever meet, and changes slowly on purpose.
DISTROS.specs: ISO: netinst ≈ 0.7 GB (downloads the rest) · VM: 2–4 GB RAM, 20 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: The installer asks more questions than Ubuntu's, and if you skip selecting a desktop environment you will boot to a bare text login. That is a choice you made, not an error.
DISTROS.steps:
• Pick Graphical install from the boot menu, then set language, location and keyboard.
  • It configures the network automatically (the VM's NAT connection just works), then asks for a hostname.
  • Set a root password, then create your everyday user account and its password — two separate accounts, that is normal here.
  • Partitioning: choose "Guided — use entire disk", pick the virtual disk, and "All files in one partition".
  • Software selection: tick a desktop environment (GNOME is the default; Xfce is lighter) plus "standard system utilities" — skip this screen and you get no desktop.
  • Say yes to installing the GRUB bootloader on the disk, reboot, and remove the ISO.
DISTROS.note: The netinst image is small because it downloads packages during install, so keep the VM's network connected. Modern Debian images include the firmware real hardware needs, so the old "wifi driver hunt" is mostly history. Debian is also the base Ubuntu, Mint and Kali are built on — learn it once and half this library feels familiar.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
DISTROS.inst:
sudo apt install vlc
# any package by name: git, gimp, htop…

DISTROS.name: Ubuntu
DISTROS.keys: first beginner server desktop apt snap
DISTROS.best: Your first distro. The biggest community, the most tutorials, and nearly every guide on the internet quietly assumes it.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 6 GB · VM: 4 GB RAM, 2 cores, 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: The first boot can feel slow while it indexes and updates. Some apps ship as Snaps and open a touch slowly the first time — normal, not broken.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO and choose "Install Ubuntu" (or "Try Ubuntu" first to look around — the installer icon is on the desktop).
  • Language and keyboard layout, then how updates and third-party drivers/codecs should be handled — ticking the third-party box saves errands later.
  • Installation type: "Erase disk and install Ubuntu" — inside a VM, that disk is the virtual file, not your computer.
  • Pick your time zone on the map, then create your user: name, computer name, username and password.
  • Let it copy and finish, click "Restart now", and remove the ISO when it asks.
DISTROS.note: When something goes wrong, search your exact error plus "Ubuntu" — with this many users, someone has already had your problem and written the answer. In VirtualBox, "Ubuntu (64-bit)" is the version to pick when creating the VM.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
DISTROS.inst:
sudo apt install vlc
# or use the App Center for a graphical store

DISTROS.name: Linux Mint
DISTROS.keys: first beginner windows old laptop apt
DISTROS.best: Windows refugees. The Cinnamon desktop has the taskbar, start menu and window habits your hands already know.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 2.8 GB · VM: 4 GB RAM (2 works), 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Do not bring Windows habits with you: no .exe installers, no downloading random setup files. Software comes from the built-in Software Manager.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot into the live desktop first — Mint always lets you look before you leap. Double-click "Install Linux Mint".
  • Language, keyboard, then tick the box to install multimedia codecs.
  • Installation type: "Erase disk and install Linux Mint" (in a VM that is only the virtual disk).
  • Time zone, then your name, username and password.
  • Reboot when it finishes and remove the ISO/USB when prompted.
DISTROS.note: After install, run the Update Manager once and open the Welcome screen's Driver Manager — Mint is deliberately boring after that, which is the compliment it wants. In VirtualBox, version "Ubuntu (64-bit)" is the closest match, since Mint is built on Ubuntu.
DISTROS.upd:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
# or click the shield icon: Update Manager
DISTROS.inst:
sudo apt install vlc
# or browse the Software Manager app

DISTROS.name: Pop!_OS
DISTROS.best: Made by the laptop maker System76, for anyone: a clean, keyboard-friendly desktop with the friendliest NVIDIA support in the business — there is a separate download with the NVIDIA driver already in it.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 2.5–4 GB (NVIDIA image is bigger) · VM: 4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Two downloads exist: standard and NVIDIA. On real hardware with an NVIDIA graphics card, get the NVIDIA one. In a VM it makes no difference.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO into the live desktop, choose language and keyboard.
  • Choose "Clean Install" — this erases the selected disk (only the virtual disk, in VirtualBox).
  • Optionally enable drive encryption on a real laptop; skip it in a learning VM.
  • It installs, then reboots into a short welcome flow where you create your user account and pick your theme.
DISTROS.note: Pop!_OS shines on real hardware: hybrid-graphics switching, the optional NVIDIA image, and the Pop!_Shop store. Its window tiling mode is a quiet productivity superpower — try it from the top-right menu once you are settled.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
DISTROS.inst:
sudo apt install vlc
# or browse the Pop!_Shop store

DISTROS.name: MX Linux
DISTROS.best: The revival specialist: MX takes laptops that Windows has given up on and makes them feel responsive again, with a toolbox of friendly utilities (MX Tools) no other distro matches.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 2 GB · VM: 2 GB RAM, 20 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: MX runs beautifully live from USB, and its installer can preserve your /home folder — read each screen; the defaults are safe, the options are powerful.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the live system (it is fast — that is the point) and click the installer icon on the desktop.
  • Keyboard first, then the disk step: choose "Auto install using entire disk" for the simple path.
  • Set the computer name (defaults are fine), then create your user and set the root password.
  • It installs quickly; reboot and remove the ISO/USB.
DISTROS.note: First stop after install: MX Package Installer, which adds popular apps (including ones from outside the main repos) in one click, and the main updater in the panel. MX also makes a bootable snapshot of your whole system onto USB — a party trick worth learning later.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
DISTROS.inst:
sudo apt install vlc
# or use MX Package Installer

DISTROS.name: Kali Linux
DISTROS.best: Security learners. Hundreds of testing tools preinstalled and organised — pair it with the lab guide in this section.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 4 GB, or the ready-made VirtualBox image · VM: 4 GB RAM, 30 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: A specialist tool, not a daily driver — do not browse, bank and live in Kali. And know the shortcut: the official prebuilt VirtualBox image skips installing entirely.
DISTROS.steps:
• From the ISO, choose Graphical install. Language, location, keyboard.
  • Create your user — modern Kali runs as this ordinary user, not as root (a deliberate, good change).
  • Partitioning: "Guided — use entire disk", all files in one partition.
  • Software selection: leave the default toolset ticked for your first install; the "large" set is a big download you can add later.
  • Install GRUB on the disk, reboot, remove the ISO.
DISTROS.note: The faster VirtualBox route: Kali publishes a prebuilt VirtualBox image. Download it, import the appliance (File → Import), boot, log in — then immediately change the default password and take your "Clean Kali" snapshot. Everything Kali assumes about networking and safety is in the "Set up your first security lab" guide above.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y
DISTROS.inst:
sudo apt install <tool-name>
# most of the toolkit is already here

DISTROS.name: Parrot OS
DISTROS.best: Kali's friendlier rival: the same family of security tools, but packaged as a system you can also live in — plus privacy tooling (Tor routing options, encrypted tools) built in. Security edition for testing work, Home edition for everyday use.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 4–5 GB · VM: 4 GB RAM, 30 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Pick the right edition: Security for the toolset, Home for a daily system without it. Like Kali, it belongs in a VM for lab work, not as your bank-and-browse machine.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the live desktop and start the Install Parrot installer (Calamares).
  • Language, keyboard and time zone.
  • Disk step: "Erase disk" — in a VM, that is only the virtual disk.
  • Create your user and password, confirm the summary, install, reboot, remove the ISO.
DISTROS.note: Parrot uses its own repository on top of Debian, kept deliberately conservative about updates. Its AnonSurf tool routes traffic through Tor — know what that does and does not protect before relying on it; the honest explanation is in the "Which distro for which job" article.
DISTROS.upd:
sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade
# Parrot provides a one-command updater too:
# sudo parrot-upgrade

DISTROS.name: Tails
DISTROS.best: The amnesiac: Tails runs entirely from a USB stick, routes everything through Tor, and forgets everything when you shut down. Built for journalists, activists, and anyone using a computer they cannot trust.
DISTROS.specs: USB image ≈ 1.5 GB · Runs from USB · 2 USB sticks recommended for install
DISTROS.watch: Tails is not installed like other distros, and that is the point. Anything you want kept needs its encrypted Persistent Storage — and enabling it is a decision, not a default.
DISTROS.vmAlt:
Honest answer: Tails does not belong in VirtualBox. Its entire design — leave no trace on the machine — fights against a VM, whose host keeps disks, snapshots and logs. You can boot the image in a VM to look at the desktop, but do not treat that as private.

The real route is the USB route (B below) — Tails is written to a USB stick and booted directly, on almost any PC.
DISTROS.steps:
• On the Welcome Screen, choose your language and keyboard; this is also where you unlock Persistent Storage if you created it.
  • Connect to Tor when prompted — the connection assistant handles bridges if Tor is blocked on your network.
  • That is the whole "install": the desktop you reach is the system, running from the stick.
DISTROS.usbAlt:
1. From the official site, download the USB image and follow Tails' own verification steps if you can — this is software worth verifying.
  2. Write the image to a USB stick (8 GB+) with Balena Etcher. Everything on that stick is erased; the PC's disk is never touched.
  3. Restart the PC, open the boot menu (often F12, F9, Esc or F2) and boot from the USB.
  4. On the Welcome Screen, optionally create Persistent Storage — an encrypted area of the stick where files, wifi passwords and settings can survive reboots. Without it, shutdown erases everything, by design.
  5. Shut down and pull the stick out: the computer is exactly as you found it.
DISTROS.note: Because Tails resets itself, updates work differently: when a new version exists, Tails tells you at boot and upgrades the stick itself, with a manual-upgrade path (a second stick) when a release is too big for the automatic one.
DISTROS.upd:
# Tails upgrades itself: accept the upgrade prompt after boot.
# No manual apt upgrade — the system is designed to reset.
DISTROS.inst:
# Software comes from Tails' included catalogue.
# Extra apps can be added via Persistent Storage —
# read Tails' own documentation first.

DISTROS.name: Raspberry Pi OS
DISTROS.best: The official system for the Raspberry Pi: a friendly Debian-based desktop tuned for the little ARM boards, with the huge Pi community and its project tutorials behind it.
DISTROS.specs: Image written to microSD · Pi: 2 GB+ RAM recommended · VM (PC edition): 2 GB RAM, 20 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Two different things share this name. The Pi image will not run on a normal PC or in a standard VirtualBox VM — for PCs there is a separate 'Debian with Raspberry Pi Desktop' download. Match the download to the hardware.
DISTROS.vmAlt: In VirtualBox you install the PC edition: download "Debian with Raspberry Pi Desktop" from the official software page, create the VM (Debian 64-bit, 2 GB RAM, 20 GB disk), attach the ISO, and run the standard Debian graphical installer from the VirtualBox guide — language, user, "use entire disk", desktop included by default, reboot.
DISTROS.steps:
• Download Raspberry Pi Imager from the official site (Windows, Mac, Linux all fine).
  • Choose OS → Raspberry Pi OS (pick the desktop edition), choose your microSD card as storage.
  • Use Imager's settings (gear icon) to pre-set your username, password and wifi — this saves typing later.
  • Write the card. Everything on it is erased.
  • Put the card in the Pi, connect screen, keyboard and power, and it boots to the desktop (a short setup wizard finishes account and update checks).
DISTROS.note: The Imager route replaces the USB-installer dance entirely — there is no ISO-to-disk installer on the Pi itself. Everything after that is Debian: same APT, same commands, same family as Ubuntu and Mint.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade
DISTROS.inst:
sudo apt install vlc
# or browse Recommended Software in the menu

DISTROS.name: elementary OS
DISTROS.best: The design student's distro: a coherent, opinionated, genuinely beautiful desktop (Pantheon) with its own curated app store. If you care how a system feels, start here.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 3 GB · VM: 4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: The download page suggests a payment — it is pay-what-you-want; entering a custom amount of 0 is an offered option. Also: elementary is minimal by design, and its AppCenter favours apps built for it.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO, pick language and keyboard.
  • Choose "Erase Disk and Install" for the clean path (in a VM, only the virtual disk is erased), with optional encryption on real hardware.
  • It installs and reboots into a short setup: create your user account, pick light/dark and accent colour.
DISTROS.note: Updates and apps arrive through AppCenter; under the hood it is Ubuntu LTS, so the terminal commands and most Ubuntu help pages apply. Its multitasking view and picture-in-picture mode are worth the first tour.
DISTROS.upd:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
# or let AppCenter handle it
DISTROS.inst:
sudo apt install vlc
# or search AppCenter (Flatpak)

DISTROS.name: Zorin OS
DISTROS.best: Built to receive defectors: Zorin Appearance switches the desktop between Windows-like and macOS-like layouts in one click, and it detects Windows apps you try to run and suggests alternatives.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 3.5 GB · VM: 4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: There is a paid 'Pro' edition with extra layouts and bundled apps; the free Core edition is the full operating system — the one to install.
DISTROS.steps:

  • Tick third-party drivers/codecs, then "Erase disk and install Zorin OS" in a VM (or "Install alongside" on a real dual-boot).
  • Time zone, user account, install, reboot, remove the ISO/USB.
  • After first login, open Zorin Appearance and pick the layout that matches your muscle memory.
DISTROS.note: Zorin is Ubuntu-based, so APT and Ubuntu help pages all apply. Its Windows App Support helper (Wine-based) is honest about being a bridge, not a promise — most switchers end up on native apps within a month.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
DISTROS.inst:
sudo apt install vlc
# or the Software store

DISTROS.name: Linux Lite
DISTROS.keys: old laptop lightweight windows beginner apt
DISTROS.best: Aimed squarely at Windows users with modest PCs: Xfce kept deliberately familiar, helpful 'Lite Tweaks' tools for cleaning and fixing, and documentation written for non-experts.

sudo apt install vlc

DISTROS.name: Peppermint OS
DISTROS.best: A featherweight Debian base with a clever idea: web apps as first-class desktop apps. Its Kumo tool turns any website into a windowed 'app' — perfect for low-storage machines that live in the browser anyway.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 2.5 GB · VM: 2 GB RAM, 20 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Peppermint installs lean on purpose; some things you expect preinstalled arrive when you ask for them. The Welcome screen is the tour guide — take it.

  • Disk step: "Erase disk" for the simple path (virtual disk only, inside a VM).
  • Create your user, install, reboot, remove the ISO/USB.
DISTROS.note: Old Peppermints were Ubuntu-based; current ones are Debian-based — download the current image from the official site and this guide still fits. After install, updates and software are standard APT.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

DISTROS.name: Devuan
DISTROS.best: Debian, forked at one specific decision: no systemd. Devuan lets you pick your init system (sysvinit, OpenRC, runit) and is the refuge for admins who want Debian's stability with the classic init model.
DISTROS.specs: ISO: installer or live ≈ 1–4 GB by edition · VM: 2 GB RAM, 20 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: This distro exists for people with a formed opinion about init systems. If you do not have one yet, plain Debian is the simpler start — Devuan will still be here when you do.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the installer ISO: language, keyboard, network.
  • Create user and root password (Debian-style), partition with "Guided — use entire disk".
  • On expert installs you choose the init system; the standard path picks a sane default.
  • Software selection: tick a desktop if you want one, install GRUB, reboot, remove the ISO.
DISTROS.note: Package-for-package, Devuan tracks Debian, so Debian documentation mostly applies — the difference is under the floorboards, in how services are started and supervised.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

DISTROS.name: antiX
DISTROS.best: The floor of the possible: antiX runs a full desktop in a few hundred megabytes of RAM, reviving machines from the Windows XP era. It is also proudly systemd-free and lightning-fast live from USB.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 1–2 GB by edition · VM: 1 GB RAM, 10 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: The 'full' edition is the one to download; 'base' and 'core' are for builders. On truly ancient PCs the 32-bit image still exists — one of the last distros to offer one.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the live system (it starts fast, even from USB) and run the antiX installer from the menu.
  • Choose the disk and "auto-install" for the simple path, or partition by hand.
  • Set the computer name, create your user, set passwords, install, reboot, remove the ISO/USB.
DISTROS.note: antiX shares MX Linux's toolbox DNA, and its control centre covers most tasks without a terminal. It is the honest recommendation when a machine has 2 GB of RAM or less — see the "old laptops" section of the which-distro article.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

DISTROS.name: Deepin

DISTROS.note: Deepin is Debian-based, so APT works as usual, but its own App Store is the intended front door. The Control Center centralises settings the way a phone does — one of the friendliest in Linux.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

sudo apt install vlc

DISTROS.name: KDE neon

DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 2.5 GB · VM: 4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk

pkcon install vlc
# or browse Discover

sudo apt install vlc

DISTROS.name: Vanilla OS
DISTROS.keys: vanilla os immutable debian gnome apx
DISTROS.best: An immutable, Debian-based distro with a near-stock GNOME desktop, smart updates that only apply when you're idle, and APX — a tool that lets you install packages from Debian, Fedora, Arch and more inside containers.
