DISTROS.watch: Vanilla OS 2's documentation mixes v1 and v2 material, so double-check any APX command against the current docs before trusting it.
DISTROS.steps:
• VirtualBox: create a VM (4 GB RAM, 50 GB disk), boot the ISO into the live GNOME session, run the Vanilla Installer, and follow it through language, keyboard and disk setup, then the First Setup wizard for your user account.
  • Real PC: write the ISO to USB, boot, and run the same installer — WARNING: choosing to use the whole disk erases everything on it. Back up first; manual partitioning is available if you want to dual-boot, but read each screen carefully.
DISTROS.note: Vanilla OS 2 'Orchid' is the current release line; updates are otherwise automatic on a schedule you pick in First Setup.
DISTROS.upd: sudo vso trigger-update --now (then reboot)

DISTROS.name: Whonix
DISTROS.keys: whonix tor anonymity privacy gateway workstation
DISTROS.best: A Debian-based anonymity system built as two VMs: a Gateway that forces all traffic through Tor, and a Workstation where you actually work — so even malware in the Workstation cannot learn your real IP address. For journalists, researchers and privacy-focused users; not a daily driver.
DISTROS.specs: Two VM images ≈ 3 GB combined · at least 4 GB RAM total, 30 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Never use the Workstation while the Gateway is off, and never run other software in the Gateway — one leak breaks the whole model. Also note the current desktop is LXQt, not the older Xfce images some guides still show.
DISTROS.steps:
• VirtualBox only: download both Whonix LXQt images (Gateway and Workstation) from whonix.org and verify the signatures, then in VirtualBox use File → Import Appliance for the Gateway first, then the Workstation — do not change any settings on import, per the official wiki.
  • Start the Gateway first, click through setup and Connect to Tor, then start the Workstation.
  • There is no supported install-on-a-real-PC route for beginners — installing it as your main OS defeats its design. Run it inside VirtualBox on your existing OS.
DISTROS.note: Whonix is designed for VirtualBox, not bare metal — that is the whole point of the Gateway/Workstation split.
DISTROS.upd: In each VM (Gateway and Workstation separately): sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade
DISTROS.inst: Tor Browser is preinstalled in the Workstation

DISTROS.name: Arch Linux
DISTROS.best: People who want to understand every layer because they assembled every layer. The Arch Wiki is the best Linux documentation on Earth.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 1 GB · VM: 2–4 GB RAM, 20 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Honest warning: there is no classic point-and-click installer. You partition disks and install packages by hand (the archinstall script softens this a lot). A brilliant teacher, a poor first distro.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO and you land at a root prompt — no desktop, no wizard. Connect the network (automatic in a VM; iwctl for wifi on real hardware).
  • Partition the disk with fdisk or cfdisk, format the partitions, and mount them under /mnt.
  • Install the base system: pacstrap -K /mnt base linux linux-firmware, then generate the filesystem table with genfstab.
  • arch-chroot /mnt into your new system: set time zone, language, hostname, root password, and install a bootloader (GRUB) — then install a desktop if you want one.
  • Exit, unmount, reboot, remove the ISO: you boot into the system you built.
DISTROS.note: The middle path: the bundled archinstall script turns all of this into a guided menu and produces a genuine Arch system — a reasonable first Arch install, after which the manual route teaches you what the script did. Either way, the Arch Wiki installation guide is the authority; follow it, not memory, not a video. Do Arch in a VM, with snapshots, after the 15-commands guide feels easy.
DISTROS.upd: sudo pacman -Syu
DISTROS.inst:
sudo pacman -S firefox
# community packages: the AUR, via an AUR helper

DISTROS.name: Manjaro
DISTROS.best: Arch's rolling software with an installer, a graphical package manager and sensible defaults: Manjaro holds Arch packages back briefly for extra testing, then hands them over with the rough edges filed down.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 3.5–4 GB by edition · VM: 4 GB RAM, 30 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Manjaro is Arch-based, not Arch: its repos are its own and updates arrive in tested batches. Mixing in raw Arch repos is how Manjaro systems break — use Pamac and the AUR tab instead.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the live desktop (pick your edition: Xfce, Plasma or GNOME) and start the installer (Calamares).
  • Language, keyboard, time zone.
  • Disk: "Erase disk" for the simple path — Manjaro can set up swap and snapshots for you.
  • Create your user (it can also set up the same password for admin), install, reboot, remove the ISO/USB.
  • First login: the Welcome screen offers the update and the hardware driver tool — run both.
DISTROS.note: Pamac, Manjaro's graphical manager, can also enable the AUR (the community's vast extra catalogue) in its settings — powerful, and worth reading the on-screen cautions before enabling. Kernel switching is a Manjaro party trick: the Settings Manager keeps several kernels installed side by side.
DISTROS.upd:
sudo pacman -Syu
# or open Pamac (Add/Remove Software)
DISTROS.inst:
sudo pacman -S vlc
# or search Pamac

DISTROS.name: EndeavourOS
DISTROS.best: Arch with the installation done and nothing else in your way: a small, friendly layer over near-vanilla Arch, a welcoming community, and a terminal-centric philosophy that teaches as it goes.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 3 GB · VM: 4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: No graphical package manager by default — updates are a terminal habit here (one short command, below). That is the intended experience, not a missing feature.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the live session and start the installer (Calamares) from the Welcome app.
  • Choose Offline (installs the Xfce desktop from the ISO) or Online (downloads your pick of desktops and up-to-date packages).
  • Language, keyboard, time zone; disk: "Erase disk" for the simple path.
  • Create your user, install, reboot, remove the ISO/USB.
DISTROS.note: EndeavourOS ships yay, an AUR helper, by default — the community repository is a first-class citizen here, with the standard AUR caution: it is community-built, so read before you install obscure packages.
DISTROS.upd:
sudo pacman -Syu
# including AUR packages: yay -Syu

DISTROS.name: Garuda Linux
DISTROS.best: Arch turned up loud: a striking dragon-themed Plasma desktop, performance tweaks and gaming tools preinstalled, Btrfs snapshots by default, and a one-command updater that maintains the whole setup.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 3.5–5 GB by edition · VM: 4 GB RAM (more is happier), 30 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Garuda's flagship look wants a reasonably modern GPU and RAM; on weak hardware pick one of its lighter editions. The dragon aesthetic is a lot — you will know in one screenshot if it is for you.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the live desktop and start the installer (Calamares): language, keyboard, time zone.
  • Disk: "Erase disk" — Garuda formats with Btrfs and sets up automatic snapshots by default.
  • Create your user, install, reboot, remove the ISO/USB.
  • First login: the Setup Assistant offers gaming and productivity bundles — pick what you actually use.
DISTROS.note: Two Garuda signatures: garuda-update (below) wraps updates with the fixes Garuda knows about, and Snapper restores yesterday's system from the boot menu if an update ever misbehaves — rolling release with a safety net, as it should be.
DISTROS.upd: garuda-update
DISTROS.inst:
sudo pacman -S vlc
# Garuda Assistant & Gamer cover bundles

DISTROS.name: CachyOS
DISTROS.desktop: KDE Plasma default · your pick at install
DISTROS.best: Arch rebuilt for speed: packages compiled for modern CPUs (x86-64-v3/v4), a tuned kernel with extra schedulers, and a friendly installer that lets you pick your desktop — plus a handheld edition for Steam Deck-style devices.
DISTROS.specs: ISO: desktop edition from cachyos.org · VM: 4 GB RAM, 30 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: The speed comes from CPU-optimised builds: very old CPUs without x86-64-v3 support will not get the optimised repositories. Rolling like Arch, so keep snapshots or backups if you value a quiet life.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the live desktop and start the installer: bootloader, language, keyboard, time zone.
  • Disk: "Erase disk" for the simple path — Btrfs is the default, which enables snapshots.
  • Pick your desktop (KDE Plasma is the default) and any extra packages, create your user, install, reboot, remove the USB.
DISTROS.note: CachyOS's hardware tool handles drivers and kernel flavours for you, and its welcome app ranks mirrors and applies updates. Underneath it is plain Arch: the Arch Wiki mostly applies, and updates are the one command below.
DISTROS.upd: sudo pacman -Syu

DISTROS.name: Artix Linux
DISTROS.best: Arch's rolling packages on your choice of init system — OpenRC, runit, s6 or dinit instead of systemd. For users who want both the AUR-era ecosystem and the classic init model.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 1–2 GB by edition · VM: 2–4 GB RAM, 20 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: You must pick an init system before downloading — the ISOs are separate. New to the question? OpenRC is the most documented of the four.
DISTROS.steps:
• Download the ISO for your chosen init system (and desktop, if you want the graphical edition).
  • GUI editions: boot the live desktop and run the Calamares installer — language, keyboard, disk ("Erase disk"), user, done.
  • Base edition: a manual, Arch-style install (partition, mount, basestrap, configure) described in Artix's own wiki.
  • Reboot, remove the ISO, and log into your system.
DISTROS.note: Artix mirrors Arch's repositories plus its own, so Pacman habits and most Arch Wiki pages carry over — except anything that assumes systemd, which is rather the point.
DISTROS.upd: sudo pacman -Syu

DISTROS.name: Fedora Workstation
DISTROS.best: Developers who want recent software without living on the edge. Fedora is where next year's enterprise Linux is rehearsed.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 2.4 GB · VM: 4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: A new release lands roughly every six months and upgrades are part of the deal. Some media codecs are not included by default — the RPM Fusion repo is the standard add-on.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the live desktop, click "Install to Hard Drive" — Fedora's installer is called Anaconda and works spokes, not a straight line.
  • Language first, then visit Installation Destination: pick the disk and accept automatic partitioning (in a VM the whole virtual disk is used).
  • Back at the hub, Begin Installation. While it works, set the root password and create your user from the same screen.
  • Reboot, remove the ISO, and finish the GNOME welcome (online accounts are optional — skip freely).
DISTROS.note: Package commands differ from the Debian family: dnf instead of apt — same ideas, different uniform. Add RPM Fusion after install if you need extra media codecs or NVIDIA drivers; it is the community-standard companion repo.
DISTROS.upd: sudo dnf upgrade

DISTROS.name: Red Hat Enterprise Linux
DISTROS.best: The commercial benchmark: a decade of support per release, certified hardware and software, and a support line businesses pay for. Most 'enterprise Linux' job adverts mean this, or one of its rebuilds below.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 10 GB (full) or smaller boot image · VM: 4 GB RAM, 30 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: RHEL needs a Red Hat account: the free Developer Subscription (for individuals, from developers.redhat.com) is the way in — the installer asks you to register the system so it can receive updates.
DISTROS.steps:
• Download the ISO from Red Hat (account required), boot it, and choose "Install Red Hat Enterprise Linux".
  • Anaconda opens: language, then the spokes — Installation Destination (pick the disk, automatic layout), and Software Selection ("Server with GUI" suits a first install).
  • Set the root password and create an administrative user while packages install.
  • Reboot, remove the ISO, and complete registration if the installer did not already — an unregistered system cannot update.
DISTROS.note: Everything from Fedora's world applies, slowed down and guaranteed: DNF, .rpm packages, SELinux enforcing by default (leave it on; it is a security feature, not an obstacle). For learning without any account at all, Rocky or AlmaLinux below are the same shape, free.
DISTROS.upd: sudo dnf upgrade
DISTROS.inst:
sudo dnf install vlc
# note: smaller catalogue than Fedora's

DISTROS.name: CentOS Stream
DISTROS.best: The development stream of RHEL itself: updates land in CentOS Stream first, then in RHEL. Server-focused, community-run by Red Hat, and the right choice if your work tracks where RHEL is heading.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 4–11 GB by image type · VM: 2–4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Not the old CentOS Linux: that version-based line ended, and Stream replaced it as a rolling-preview. Advice written for 'CentOS 7/8' mostly does not apply here.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO into Anaconda: language and keyboard.
  • Installation Destination: pick the disk, automatic partitioning.
  • Software Selection: "Server" for a headless box, "Server with GUI" if you want a desktop in the VM.
  • Set root password, create your user, install, reboot, remove the ISO.
DISTROS.note: Stream teaches the Red Hat family's ways — DNF, systemd services, SELinux — on a moving but managed track. It is a server system: expect a minimal default and to add what you need.
DISTROS.upd: sudo dnf upgrade

DISTROS.name: Rocky Linux
DISTROS.best: A bug-for-bug RHEL rebuild, founded by one of CentOS's original creators after CentOS changed direction. Free, community-governed, and built for production servers that want RHEL's behaviour without the subscription.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 2–11 GB by image type · VM: 2–4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: 'Minimal' images are command-line only. First time? Take the DVD/boot image and choose 'Server with GUI' during install — you can strip it down later.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO into Anaconda: language and keyboard.
  • Installation Destination: choose the disk, accept automatic partitioning.
  • Software Selection: Server with GUI (or plain Server for a headless VM).
  • Root password + administrative user, install, reboot, remove the ISO.
DISTROS.note: Rocky's promise is discipline: it tracks RHEL release for release, so RHEL documentation and skills transfer exactly — which is why it is a favourite for learning the enterprise stack and for real production servers alike.
DISTROS.upd: sudo dnf upgrade

DISTROS.name: AlmaLinux
DISTROS.best: The other great RHEL rebuild: community-owned (a non-profit foundation), backed originally by CloudLinux, and interchangeable with RHEL in behaviour. Rocky and Alma are twins in purpose — pick either with confidence.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 2–11 GB by image type · VM: 2–4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: As with Rocky, minimal images are CLI-only. AlmaLinux also offers ELevate, its in-place upgrade tool between major versions — rare in this family and worth knowing exists.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO into Anaconda: language and keyboard.
  • Installation Destination: pick the disk, automatic partitioning.
  • Software Selection: Server with GUI for a desktop in the VM, Server for headless.
  • Root password + administrative user, install, reboot, remove the ISO.
DISTROS.note: Alma's governance is its pitch: no single company can change its direction, which is exactly what the CentOS episode taught the community to want. Day to day, it is DNF, systemd and SELinux — the full Red Hat family skillset.
DISTROS.upd: sudo dnf upgrade

DISTROS.name: Nobara
DISTROS.best: Fedora after a gamer has fixed everything: maintained by GloriousEggroll (of Proton-GE fame), Nobara pre-applies the codecs, drivers, kernel patches and OBS/game tooling that Fedora leaves as homework.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 3.5–4.5 GB by edition · VM: 4 GB RAM, 30 GB disk (real hardware shows it best)
DISTROS.watch: Pick the edition matching your GPU — there are NVIDIA and standard images. Nobara is a passion project on Fedora's base: version upgrades follow its own guides, so read the release notes each cycle.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the live desktop and start the installer: language, keyboard, time zone.
  • Disk: "Erase disk" for the simple path (virtual disk only, in a VM).
  • Create your user, install, reboot, remove the ISO/USB.
  • First login: the Welcome app handles driver checks and offers the gaming toolset — let it.
DISTROS.note: Steam, Lutris, Proton-GE and capture tools are either present or one click away, which is the entire value proposition: on Nobara the "Linux gaming setup guide" is mostly already done. Underneath, it is Fedora — DNF commands and Fedora knowledge apply.
DISTROS.upd:
sudo dnf upgrade
# Nobara also ships its own updater in the menu

DISTROS.name: Bazzite
DISTROS.best: A Fedora Atomic image rebuilt as a games console: Steam and the Deck-style gaming mode included, system updates atomic (all-or-nothing, so they cannot half-break), aimed at PCs and handhelds alike.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 6–8 GB by image · VM: 4 GB RAM, 40 GB disk (real hardware recommended)
DISTROS.watch: Bazzite is image-based: you do not install system software the usual DNF way. Apps come from Flatpak (Discover), and advanced tweaks use its ujust command recipes — different habits, deliberately.
DISTROS.steps:
• Download the image for your hardware (desktop/handheld, GPU type) — the site picker matters here.
  • Boot the ISO and run the installer: language, keyboard, pick the disk — the whole disk is the simple path.
  • Create your user, install, reboot, remove the ISO/USB.
  • First boot lands in a Steam-Deck-like setup; sign into Steam, then find the normal desktop one menu away.
DISTROS.note: Updates arrive as whole new system images and apply on reboot — if one ever misbehaves, the previous image is still there to boot. It is the safest update model in this library, borrowed from how consoles and phones already work.
DISTROS.upd:
# Updates are automatic (image-based).
# By hand: rpm-ostree upgrade, then reboot.
# Extras and tweaks: ujust
DISTROS.inst:
flatpak install flathub org.videolan.VLC
# apps come from Discover/Flathub

DISTROS.name: Oracle Linux
DISTROS.desktop: GNOME default · server installs often headless
DISTROS.keys: enterprise server oracle database dnf rhel
DISTROS.best: Oracle's enterprise Linux, binary-compatible with Red Hat Enterprise Linux, for servers, databases and Oracle workloads. It ships Oracle's Unbreakable Enterprise Kernel alongside a Red Hat-compatible kernel, plus zero-downtime kernel patching.
DISTROS.specs: ISO: from oracle.com/linux · VM: 2 vCPUs, 4 GB RAM, 20 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Enterprise/server focus, not a first-desktop pick. Sticking to Oracle's kernels and tools matters most if you run Oracle databases; otherwise it behaves like RHEL.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO and follow the Anaconda installer: language, keyboard, time zone.
  • Disk: "Erase disk" for the simple path — this destroys everything on that drive, so back up first and double-check the target disk.
  • Choose your software selection (server or workstation), create your user, install, reboot, remove the USB.
DISTROS.note: Underneath it is RHEL-compatible: DNF and RPM workflows, SELinux and the RHEL documentation mostly apply.
DISTROS.upd: sudo dnf update -y

DISTROS.name: Asahi Linux
DISTROS.keys: apple silicon mac m1 m2 fedora asahi
DISTROS.best: The polished Linux for Apple Silicon Macs (M1/M2, with M3/M4 support maturing) — the only serious way to run Linux natively on an Apple Silicon Mac. For Mac owners who want Linux without giving up macOS.
DISTROS.specs: Apple Silicon Mac only · installer downloads the system image
DISTROS.watch: Check the device-support page for your exact Mac model before installing — a few features are still missing per model, and M3/M4 support is newer than M1/M2.
DISTROS.steps:
• Fully update macOS first, then in Terminal run the official installer: curl https://alx.sh | sh.
  • It walks you through choosing a desktop (KDE Plasma or GNOME) and how much disk space to give Linux (it shrinks the macOS container; macOS stays intact), then downloads and installs.
  • Reboot holding the power button to pick macOS or Linux at startup.
  • There is no VirtualBox route — Asahi does not run in a VM on a Mac this way, and it does not run on PCs or Intel Macs at all.
DISTROS.note: Asahi keeps macOS intact, so no erase-disk warning applies here — but you are still partitioning a Mac, so back up first anyway.
DISTROS.upd: sudo dnf upgrade --refresh

DISTROS.name: Fedora Silverblue
DISTROS.best: Fedora's immutable desktop: the base system is a read-only image that updates atomically, so a bad update can be rolled back in one reboot. For tinkerers and developers who want Fedora's freshness without ever breaking their system.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 4 GB · VM: 4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Updates only take effect after a reboot, and a rebase to a new Fedora release does not touch your Flatpaks — update those separately.
DISTROS.steps:
• VirtualBox: create a VM (4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk), boot the Silverblue ISO and follow the Fedora installer (language, keyboard, Automatic partitioning on the virtual disk, user account), then reboot into GNOME.
  • Real PC: write the ISO to USB, boot, and run the same installer — WARNING: Automatic partitioning on a real PC erases the selected disk. Back up first, or choose custom partitioning to dual-boot.
DISTROS.note: The immutable model changes how you install software: prefer Flatpaks for apps, and treat layering packages onto the base image as the exception, not the habit.
DISTROS.upd: rpm-ostree upgrade (then reboot to boot into the new image)

DISTROS.name: openSUSE Tumbleweed
DISTROS.best: The rolling release with a grown-up safety net: every package is tested by openQA before release, and the Btrfs+Snapper setup snapshots your system before updates, so a bad one is undone from the boot menu.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 4.5 GB · VM: 4 GB RAM, 30 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Rolling means the update command is different here: zypper dup, not a plain update (see First commands) — it upgrades the whole distribution each time, which is exactly what you want on Tumbleweed.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO into the YaST installer: language and keyboard (it detects most of this for you).
  • The "System Role" screen picks the personality — Desktop with KDE/GNOME/Xfce, or Server.
  • Partitioning: accept the guided proposal (Btrfs with snapshots on the system disk — say yes, it is the point).
  • Create your user (it can double as administrator), confirm the summary screen, install, reboot, remove the ISO.
DISTROS.note: Two tools define openSUSE: YaST, a control centre that can configure nearly everything graphically or in text, and Snapper, whose snapshots you will find in the boot menu and in YaST. Learn those two and Tumbleweed feels less like rolling risk and more like rolling insurance.
DISTROS.upd: sudo zypper refresh && sudo zypper dup

DISTROS.name: openSUSE Leap
DISTROS.best: Tumbleweed's calm sibling: a fixed-release distro sharing its core with SUSE Linux Enterprise, maintained on a predictable cadence. For SUSE-family stability at work or on a home server, this is it.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 4.5 GB · VM: 4 GB RAM, 30 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Leap's package versions are enterprise-conservative — that is the appeal. If you find yourself wanting Tumbleweed's newness, the two share tools, so moving later is painless.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO into the YaST installer: language, keyboard.
  • Pick a System Role (Desktop with KDE/GNOME/Xfce, or Server).
  • Accept the guided partitioning proposal, create your user, review the summary, install, reboot, remove the ISO.
DISTROS.note: Everything good about openSUSE applies: YaST for configuration, Zypper for packages, Snapper snapshots. The only difference from Tumbleweed is the tempo — and tempo is a legitimate thing to choose.
DISTROS.upd: sudo zypper refresh && sudo zypper update

DISTROS.name: Gentoo
DISTROS.desktop: None by default — you build it
DISTROS.best: The final boss, proudly: Gentoo is installed by following its Handbook and compiling your system from source, tuned to your exact hardware by USE flags you choose. Nothing teaches — or costs — like it.
DISTROS.specs: Install image small; the compiling is the cost · VM: 4 GB+ RAM, 40 GB disk, patience
DISTROS.watch: Budget time honestly: the install is a project measured in hours (large desktops compile for a long while even on fast machines), and binary packages exist only for the biggest pieces. A VM install is the sane first run.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the install image (a live environment) and set up the network — automatic in a VM.
  • Partition and format the disk by hand, mount it at /mnt/gentoo.
  • Download the stage3 tarball (a pre-built base), unpack it onto the disk, and set your USE flags and options in make.conf.
  • chroot in, sync Portage, choose a profile, and build: kernel (compiled or the distribution kernel), bootloader, core tools.
  • Create your user, set passwords, exit, unmount, reboot, remove the ISO — into the system you compiled.
DISTROS.note: The Gentoo Handbook is the installer — follow it exactly, in order, for your architecture. People do Gentoo once to understand Linux at the metal, and some simply stay. Both outcomes are respected.
DISTROS.upd:
sudo emerge --sync
sudo emerge --ask --verbose --update --deep --newuse @world
DISTROS.inst:
sudo emerge --ask www-client/firefox
# software is compiled — expect a wait

DISTROS.name: Slackware
DISTROS.best: The oldest surviving distribution (1993), run by one maintainer with a famously steady hand. Slackware changes little, assumes you read, and teaches Unix the traditional way — text configuration, no hand-holding, no surprises.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 3.5 GB · VM: 2 GB RAM, 20 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: There is no dependency resolution in the classic toolset — full installs are the expected path. Also set up a mirror for slackpkg before your first update (one line in /etc/slackpkg/mirrors).
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO and log in as root at the text prompt — the screen tells you to.
  • If the disk is blank, partition it first with cfdisk.
  • Run setup: pick the target partition, choose a full install when asked for the package series (the honest default for newcomers).
  • Configure the bootloader (ELILO/LILO), network, timezone and root password in the setup flow's final screens.
  • Reboot, remove the ISO, and create your everyday user with adduser before settling in.
DISTROS.note: Slackware's stability secret is restraint: vanilla packages, minimal patching, releases when they are ready. Systems installed in the 2000s were upgraded for decades — that is the culture you are joining.
DISTROS.upd:
slackpkg update && slackpkg upgrade-all
# run as root; pick a mirror first
DISTROS.inst:
slackpkg install <package>
# most software: the full install already has it

DISTROS.name: Void Linux
DISTROS.best: A rolling distro built entirely from scratch by its own community: its own package manager (XBPS, fast), the runit init system (tiny, transparent), and a choice of glibc or musl. Feels like Arch's quieter sibling.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 0.6–1 GB · VM: 2 GB RAM, 15 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Rolling and DIY: services are enabled by linking them yourself (one command, below in spirit — the installer notes cover the base). Also choose deliberately between glibc (maximum compatibility) and musl (maximum lean) images.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the live image, log in (the image prints its credentials: usually anon or root with password voidlinux).
  • Run sudo void-installer and walk its menus: keyboard, network, source, hostname.
  • Partition the disk inside the installer, set the filesystem mount points, and let it install the base system.
  • Set the root password and your user when prompted; install the bootloader.
  • Reboot, remove the ISO, and log in — then enable the services you want, runit-style (ln -s /etc/sv/<service> /var/service/).
DISTROS.note: XBPS is genuinely quick, and Void's repositories are rolling but curated for stability. The musl edition is a favourite for containers and minimal systems; desktop users usually want glibc for proprietary software compatibility.
DISTROS.upd: sudo xbps-install -Su

DISTROS.name: NixOS
DISTROS.best: The radical one: your entire system — packages, services, users — is declared in one configuration file, and the OS builds itself from that declaration. Rollback to yesterday's system is a boot-menu entry. Developers and reproducibility obsessives swear by it.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 2.5 GB · VM: 4 GB RAM, 30 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Throw away your package-manager reflexes: you do not 'install' apps onto NixOS the normal way — you declare them. The first week bends your brain; the payoff is a machine you can rebuild from one file.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO and the graphical installer starts: language, keyboard, time zone.
  • Choose your desktop (GNOME, Plasma, or none), then the disk step: "Erase disk" for the simple path.
  • Create your user, install, reboot, remove the ISO.
  • Your system now lives in /etc/nixos/configuration.nix — edit it, and run the rebuild command below to change anything.
DISTROS.note: Try software without committing: nix-shell -p <package> gives you a temporary shell with it, gone when you exit. Every rebuild keeps the previous generations in the boot menu — that is the rollback that makes NixOS users so calm.
DISTROS.upd:
sudo nix-channel --update
sudo nixos-rebuild switch
DISTROS.inst:
# Declare it: add the package to
# environment.systemPackages in configuration.nix,
# then: sudo nixos-rebuild switch
# Or try it first: nix-shell -p vlc

DISTROS.name: Alpine Linux
DISTROS.best: The 5-megabyte miracle behind half the world's Docker images: musl libc, BusyBox utilities, and a security-first minimalism. As a desktop it is a hobbyist's choice; for containers and lean servers it is an industry default.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 0.2–0.9 GB by edition · VM: 1 GB RAM, 8 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Alpine uses musl, not glibc: some prebuilt commercial software will not run on it. For a server/container that rarely matters; for a desktop it decides everything. The 'extended' ISO is the one with useful extras offline.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO and log in as root (no password on the live image).
  • Run setup-alpine and answer its questions: keyboard, hostname, network interface (automatic in a VM), time zone.
  • Create your user when offered, pick the package mirror it suggests, then choose the disk and the "sys" mode (a normal disk install).
  • It installs in about a minute. Reboot, remove the ISO, log in.
  • Want a desktop? Add it after: Alpine's wiki documents setup-desktop.
DISTROS.note: apk is quick and its package files are refreshingly readable. If you meet Alpine inside Docker (likely), everything here applies — the same commands run your containers.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apk update && sudo apk upgrade

DISTROS.name: Solus
DISTROS.best: A rolling distro built from scratch for home desktops, home of the Budgie desktop: curated (software is picked and tested rather than merely mirrored), stateless in design, and aimed at people who just want a handsome system that keeps itself current.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 2.5–3.5 GB by edition · VM: 4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Curated means smaller: if your favourite obscure app is missing, the Software Center takes requests — and Flatpak covers the gaps.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the live desktop of your chosen edition and click the installer.
  • Language, keyboard, time zone.
  • Disk: automatic partitioning of the whole disk is the simple path ("Erase disk" equivalent).
  • Create your user, install, reboot, remove the ISO/USB.
DISTROS.note: Solus is neither Debian, Arch nor Red Hat family — its own thing, with its own package tools (below). After install, the Software Center handles most needs graphically; updates arrive continuously with the rolling model, tested weekly by the project.
DISTROS.upd: sudo eopkg up
DISTROS.inst:
sudo eopkg it vlc
# or the Software Center

DISTROS.name: Mageia
DISTROS.best: The community fork of the beloved Mandriva, carrying its traditions forward: a famously friendly installer and the Mageia Control Center, one of the best graphical system-administration panels Linux has ever had.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 4 GB · VM: 4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Mageia releases on its own measured schedule and values stability; if you want frantic newness, look at the rolling shelves of this library instead.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO (or a live edition) and start the installer — it is the classic, well-loved DrakX flow.
  • Language, keyboard, then partitioning: "Use entire disk" for the simple path.
  • Choose your desktop when the package groups are offered (Plasma is the flagship).
  • Create your user and root password, let it install, reboot — a summary screen lets you tune network and services before first boot.
DISTROS.note: After install, the Mageia Control Center is your cockpit: software, hardware, network sharing, firewalls — a control-panel completeness Windows users find oddly comforting. Package management is urpmi by tradition, with DNF also supported.
DISTROS.upd:
sudo urpmi --auto-update
# (DNF users: sudo dnf upgrade)

DISTROS.name: PCLinuxOS
DISTROS.best: A long-running community distro with one goal: easy. It rolls (continuously updated), uses the Synaptic graphical package manager over an RPM base, and asks almost nothing of the user beyond enjoying the ride.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 2–3 GB by edition · VM: 4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Its rule is famous and strict: update fully, always — partial upgrades are unsupported. The Synaptic 'Reload → Mark All Upgrades → Apply' ritual is the way; the commands below do the same.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the live desktop — PCLinuxOS installs from the running system. Double-click Install PCLinuxOS.
  • Pick the disk and the automatic layout for the simple path.
  • Set the root password and create your user in the install flow.
  • Install, reboot, remove the ISO/USB, log in.
DISTROS.note: PCLOS preserves a classic virtue: it ships working multimedia and broad hardware support out of the box. Its magazine (yes, a community magazine) and forums are part of the charm — a distro that still feels handmade.
DISTROS.upd:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
# update fully — partial upgrades unsupported
DISTROS.inst:
sudo apt install vlc
# or Synaptic, its traditional front door

DISTROS.name: Clear Linux
DISTROS.best: Intel's own distribution, optimised relentlessly for Intel hardware and cloud workloads: fast defaults, stateless design, software in 'bundles'. Historical entry: Intel discontinued Clear Linux in July 2025 — it receives no updates and should not be a new install.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 3 GB · VM: 4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk · DISCONTINUED July 2025
DISTROS.watch: Intel ended Clear Linux in July 2025 and archived the project: no security updates will ever arrive. Do not install it as a new system — this guide stays for existing users and the historical record. Also know its model before mourning it: bundles and statelessness, with system directories reset to factory state.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the live image and launch the installer (a text-guided installer on the server image; graphical on the desktop image).
  • Language/keyboard, network check, then the target disk — the whole disk is the simple path (the installer asks for an explicit confirmation).
  • Create your user (it can be added to the admin group in the same flow), install, reboot, remove the ISO.
DISTROS.note: If anything misbehaves after your experiments, Clear's stateless design is the recovery: the OS can verify and repair its own files with swupd repair. Performance claims are its reputation — benchmarks on Intel hardware have kept it famous.
DISTROS.upd: sudo swupd update
DISTROS.inst:
sudo swupd bundle-add vlc
# software arrives as bundles, not packages

DISTROS.name: Qubes OS
DISTROS.best: Not really a distro — a security architecture: your life is split into isolated virtual machines ('qubes') — work, personal, banking, disposable — so one compromised app cannot reach the rest. Endorsed by security professionals who accept its costs.
DISTROS.specs: ISO ≈ 6 GB · Needs: 64-bit CPU with VT-x + VT-d/IOMMU, 16 GB RAM recommended · Bare metal only
DISTROS.watch: Check the hardware requirements and the Hardware Compatibility List on the official site before committing — Qubes needs virtualisation extensions with an IOMMU, and it will refuse or limp without them. It is also a lot of computer to run: 16 GB of RAM is the realistic floor.
DISTROS.vmAlt:
Honest answer: you do not install Qubes inside VirtualBox. Qubes is itself a hypervisor (Xen) that runs virtual machines all day — nesting it inside another VM is unsupported and performs terribly. Qubes is installed on bare metal, as the machine's only system. The USB route below is the install route.

To learn its ideas first without new hardware, read the project's documentation and this library's privacy article — then commit a suitable laptop when you are ready.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the USB installer: language, then the Anaconda-style hub.
  • Installation Destination: choose the disk and set disk encryption (LUKS) — on Qubes this is not optional thinking.
  • Create your user; the installer then offers the default qubes layout (sys-net, sys-firewall, personal, work, vault and disposables) — accept the defaults on a first install.
  • Reboot, enter your disk password, log in, and complete the first-boot configuration it offers.
DISTROS.usbNote: This is Qubes' natural route: write the ISO with Etcher or Rufus (DD mode), boot it, and follow the installer steps — on hardware you have checked against the requirements first. There is no try-it-in-a-VM shortcut, by deliberate design.
DISTROS.note: Daily life is colour-coded windows from different qubes sharing one screen, with networking forced through a dedicated firewall VM. Updating happens centrally: Qubes' updater refreshes dom0 and the templates (Fedora templates use DNF, Debian templates APT) so your AppVMs inherit the fixes.
DISTROS.upd:
# Use the Qubes Update tool (system tray / Qubes Manager).
# Dom0 by hand: sudo qubes-dom0-update
DISTROS.inst:
# Install software inside the TEMPLATE of the qube,
# e.g. Fedora template: sudo dnf install vlc
# Debian template: sudo apt install vlc
# then restart the AppVMs using it

DISTROS.name: Armbian
DISTROS.best: The standard system for single-board computers beyond the Raspberry Pi — Orange Pi, Banana Pi, and dozens more: Debian or Ubuntu userlands with kernels tuned per board, shipped as ready images.
DISTROS.specs: Image written to microSD/eMMC · Board-dependent · No x86 ISO
DISTROS.watch: Download the image for your exact board model — Armbian images are per-board and one board's image will not boot another. 'Supported' vs 'community' boards differ in how much testing they get; the download page says which.
DISTROS.vmAlt: Honest answer: there is no Armbian image for VirtualBox. Armbian builds are ARM images for specific boards — a standard x86 VirtualBox VM cannot boot them. The way to try Armbian is the way everyone uses it: write the image to a spare microSD card and boot the board (route B). To explore its Debian-family behaviour in a VM meanwhile, install plain Debian from this library — the userland is the same.
DISTROS.steps:
• Download the image for your exact board from the official site, and write it to a microSD card with Balena Etcher (the card is erased).
  • Insert the card, connect network and power, and give it a few minutes for the first boot (it resizes itself and generates keys).
  • Log in as root with the default password 1234 over SSH or console — you are immediately forced to change it and create your everyday user.
  • Run armbian-config for the guided setup: wifi, timezone, hardware toggles, and installing to eMMC/NVMe if your board has it.
DISTROS.note: After first boot it is the Debian family you know: APT commands below, plus armbian-config's extras. Many home servers, print servers and dashboards quietly run exactly this.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

DISTROS.name: SteamOS
DISTROS.best: The system of the Steam Deck: a console-simple gaming mode on top of an immutable Arch-based base with a full KDE desktop hiding one menu away. Millions now daily-drive Linux because of it — most without noticing.
DISTROS.specs: Recovery image for Steam Deck · Written to USB for Deck recovery
DISTROS.watch: SteamOS 3 is distributed for the Steam Deck, not as a general PC installer. The honest routes to a Deck-like PC are Bazzite (opposite page of this library) or a normal distro plus Steam — not a hacked SteamOS image.
DISTROS.vmAlt: Honest answer: SteamOS does not officially install in VirtualBox or on arbitrary PCs. Valve ships it with the Steam Deck and publishes a recovery image for the Deck only. Treat any 'SteamOS for PC' download from elsewhere as unofficial and unsupported. For the same experience on your own hardware, install Bazzite from this library — it was built for exactly that.
DISTROS.steps:
• This is the Steam Deck recovery flow: download the recovery image from Steam's official support page.
  • Write it to a USB stick (16 GB+) with Balena Etcher or Rufus — the stick is erased.
  • Power the Deck off, hold Volume Down and press Power, and pick the USB in the boot manager.
  • In the recovery desktop, choose "Reimage Steam Deck" for a full factory reinstall (this erases the Deck's storage), or the repair options for gentler fixes.
  • The Deck reboots into the standard SteamOS setup: wifi, language, Steam sign-in.
DISTROS.usbNote: Note the difference from every other guide here: this USB reinstalls a Steam Deck, not a PC. On ordinary PCs the supported experience is Deck Mode via Bazzite or Steam's own big-picture mode on any distro.
DISTROS.note: SteamOS updates arrive as system images through Steam itself (Steam button → Settings → System). Desktop-mode software comes from the Discover store as Flatpaks — the base system stays read-only, which is why Decks are so hard to break.
DISTROS.upd:
# System updates: Steam button → Settings → System
# (image-based; they apply on restart)
DISTROS.inst:
# Desktop mode → Discover store, or:
flatpak install flathub org.videolan.VLC

DISTROS.name: Endless OS
DISTROS.best: A simplified, family- and education-friendly system built for schools, labs and low- or no-connectivity settings, with a customised GNOME desktop, a read-only system image and a large offline app and content catalogue. Debian-based in origin, but in daily use that barely matters.
DISTROS.specs: Image: Basic or Full from endlessos.com · VM: 2 vCPUs, 4 GB RAM, 32 GB disk (Full images are large)
DISTROS.watch: Do not use apt to install software — the system image is read-only and apt is present but unusable for installs; apps come from the App Center (Flatpak) only.
DISTROS.steps:
• Download the Basic or Full image, write it to USB, and boot from it.
  • Follow the on-screen installer; a full install wipes the chosen drive — back up first. The Basic image needs internet for apps, while Full images carry much more offline content.
  • Create your user, finish setup, reboot, remove the USB.
DISTROS.note: System updates arrive as whole OSTree images with rollback if one fails, and apps update through the App Center.
DISTROS.upd: flatpak update

DISTROS.name: Guix System
DISTROS.best: The GNU project's advanced, declarative operating system for fully reproducible, transactional systems — every system configuration is written in Guile Scheme and every generation can be rolled back. Best for developers, free-software enthusiasts and anyone who wants to version-control their whole OS.
DISTROS.specs: ISO: installer from guix.gnu.org · VM: 2 vCPUs, 2 GB RAM, 20 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Free-software-only kernel and firmware policy: Wi-Fi and graphics hardware needing proprietary firmware may not work out of the box. Scheme-based configuration is a real learning curve.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the installer ISO and follow the guided installer: language, keyboard, partitioning, user, desktop choice.
  • Partitioning/formatting during install destroys data on the chosen disk — back up first and double-check the target disk.
  • Finish the install, reboot, remove the USB.
DISTROS.note: Guix manages system and packages declaratively: edit /etc/config.scm and reconfigure to change the system, and roll back to any previous generation if a change misbehaves.
DISTROS.upd: guix pull && sudo guix system reconfigure /etc/config.scm

DISTROS.name: OpenMandriva Lx
DISTROS.best: The independent, community-run successor of Mandriva Linux — a polished KDE Plasma desktop for general desktop users who want an RPM system outside the Fedora/Red Hat orbit.
DISTROS.specs: ISO: Plasma image from openmandriva.org · VM: 4 GB RAM, 20 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: OpenMandriva's update habit differs from Fedora's — use dsync, not dnf upgrade, for system updates.
DISTROS.steps:
• Create a Linux VM (4 GB RAM, 20 GB disk), attach the Plasma ISO from openmandriva.org, and boot the live desktop.
  • Run the Calamares installer: language, keyboard, disk step, user account, install, reboot, remove the ISO.
  • On a real PC, write the ISO to a USB stick with Balena Etcher or Rufus and boot from it — the installer steps are the same.
DISTROS.note: Erase-disk warning: choosing Erase disk wipes everything on the selected drive — back up first and disconnect drives you do not mean to touch.
DISTROS.upd: sudo dnf dsync --refresh

DISTROS.name: DietPi
DISTROS.keys: dietpi raspberry pi server sbc headless apt
DISTROS.best: A minimal, Debian-based system for single-board computers (Raspberry Pi, Odroid and others) and small servers — for home servers, media boxes and automation, not for a general desktop.
DISTROS.specs: Image: per-board image from dietpi.com · VM: official VirtualBox OVA appliance
DISTROS.watch: There is deliberately almost nothing installed at first — that is the point. If you want a desktop PC experience, this is the wrong distro; pick a desktop one from the library instead.
DISTROS.steps:
• Download the image for your exact board model (or the PC/VM VirtualBox OVA from dietpi.com for a VM) and flash it to an SD card or USB drive with Balena Etcher or Raspberry Pi Imager — or, for the OVA, import it via File, Import Appliance.
  • Insert the card or drive, power on with network connected (first boot needs the internet), and follow the one-time setup, including setting passwords, then the software picker.
DISTROS.note: Erase warning: flashing wipes the whole card or drive — check you picked the right device before starting.
DISTROS.upd: dietpi-update

DISTROS.name: Proxmox VE
DISTROS.keys: proxmox virtualisation kvm lxc server apt
DISTROS.best: A Debian-based virtualisation platform (KVM virtual machines plus LXC containers) managed through a web interface — for home labs and small servers, not a desktop OS.
DISTROS.specs: ISO from proxmox.com · Real server recommended; VM exploration only with nested virtualisation enabled
DISTROS.watch: A fresh install points at the paid enterprise repository, which fails without a subscription — switch to the free no-subscription repository first (web UI under Updates, Repositories, or by disabling pve-enterprise and adding pve-no-subscription in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/). The no-subscription repository is community-tested rather than enterprise-tested, and a fresh install shows a self-signed certificate warning in the browser — expected, but do not expose port 8006 directly to the internet.
DISTROS.steps:
• Download the ISO from Proxmox, write it to a USB stick, and boot the server from it.
  • Follow the installer: target disk, country/timezone, root password and email, management network address.
  • Reboot, then open the web UI from another machine at https://<server-IP>:8006 and log in as root.
  • In a VM only to explore the UI: enable nested virtualisation (VT-x/AMD-V) in the VM settings — guests inside it will run poorly or not at all without that.
DISTROS.note: Erase-disk warning: the installer takes over the whole selected disk and does not preserve other systems on it — back up first.
DISTROS.upd: apt update && apt dist-upgrade
DISTROS.inst: # after switching to the no-subscription repository, see the Watch out note

DISTROS.name: BlackArch Linux
DISTROS.best: An Arch-based penetration-testing distribution with thousands of categorised security tools — for security learners and testers who already know Arch. Only for authorised testing; same rule as Kali.
DISTROS.specs: ISO: Slim or netinstall from blackarch.org · VM: 4 GB RAM, 40 GB disk — the toolset is big
DISTROS.watch: Do not install every tool at once (pacman -S blackarch) — it is a huge download. Install one category at a time. Like Kali, this is a specialist toolbox, not a daily driver.
DISTROS.steps:
• Create a Linux VM (4 GB RAM, 40 GB disk), attach the Slim ISO from blackarch.org, boot into the live desktop and run the GUI installer; or boot the netinstall ISO, log in and run blackarch-install for the guided text installer.
  • On a real PC, write the ISO to a USB stick, boot, and run the installer (or blackarch-install on netinstall): keyboard, network, partitioning and packages, reboot, remove the stick.
DISTROS.note: Erase-disk warning: the installer's disk step wipes the selected drive — back up first.
DISTROS.upd: sudo pacman -Syyu
DISTROS.inst:
sudo pacman -S blackarch-<category>
# list categories: pacman -Sg | grep blackarch

DISTROS.name: Nitrux
DISTROS.best: A Debian-based, immutable, systemd-free desktop built around the Hyprland tiling Wayland compositor and its own Workspace Environment — for power users who want a distinctive, compartmentalised desktop, not a conventional one.
DISTROS.specs: ISO: per-GPU image (separate NVIDIA and AMD/Intel images) from nxos.org · VM: 4 GB RAM, 30 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Nitrux's GRUB packages and default kernel are unsigned, so an installed system may fail to boot with Secure Boot left on — disable Secure Boot or follow Nitrux's Secure Boot guide. X11 sessions are not targeted; this is a Wayland-only design.
DISTROS.steps:
• Create a Linux VM (4 GB RAM, 30 GB disk), attach the ISO for your GPU (pick the NVIDIA or AMD/Intel image correctly), boot and run the installer: language, keyboard, disk, user account, install, reboot, remove the ISO.
  • On a real PC, write the ISO to a USB stick, boot, install, reboot, remove the stick.
DISTROS.note:
Erase-disk warning: a full-disk install wipes the selected drive — back up first.

Updates use the Nitrux Update Tool System (NUTS) — Nitrux's own updater for its immutable base — and apps come via Flatpak and AppBox rather than traditional system installs.
DISTROS.upd: Use the Nitrux Update Tool System (NUTS) for base updates

DISTROS.name: Bluefin
DISTROS.keys: bluefin fedora atomic immutable flatpak universal blue
DISTROS.best: An image-based Fedora workstation with GNOME, for everyday users who want Chromebook-like reliability and developers who work in containers. The system updates as a whole image and rolls back cleanly, instead of updating package by package.
DISTROS.specs: ISO from projectbluefin.io · VM: UEFI only, 4 GB RAM, 40 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Dual-booting from the same disk is unsupported, and layering packages onto the host with rpm-ostree is discouraged. Apps come from Flathub and tools from Homebrew, and updates apply on reboot, so a pending update does nothing until you restart.
DISTROS.steps:
• Create a UEFI virtual machine (BIOS is not supported: 4 GB RAM, 40 GB disk), attach the Bluefin ISO from projectbluefin.io, boot and run the installer.
  • On a real PC, write the ISO with Fedora Media Writer (the docs say Ventoy is unsupported), boot from the USB stick and use automatic partitioning on the entire disk.
  • Create your user when asked, let it finish, reboot and remove the USB stick when prompted.
DISTROS.note:
Erase-disk warning: automatic partitioning wipes the whole drive — back up first, and do not use it on a disk you want to dual-boot from.

Bluefin's KDE sibling is Aurora, from the same Universal Blue project. Updates run automatically every 6 hours and apply on reboot.
DISTROS.upd: ujust update

DISTROS.name: Ubuntu Unity
DISTROS.keys: ubuntu unity flavour classic desktop apt
DISTROS.best: The official Ubuntu flavour that keeps the classic Unity 7 desktop, with its left-side launcher and dash, for users who never warmed to GNOME Shell. Underneath it is standard Ubuntu, so the tutorials and support all still apply.
DISTROS.specs: ISO from ubuntuunity.org · VM: 4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: Unity 7 is a maintained classic, not a modern redesign. Expect the older desktop's habits and limits, and check that any must-have GNOME-era extensions have Unity equivalents before switching.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO and choose "Install Ubuntu Unity" (or try the live session first to look around).
  • Language and keyboard layout, then how updates and third-party drivers and codecs should be handled.
  • Installation type: "Erase disk and install Ubuntu Unity" — inside a VM, that disk is the virtual one, so it is safe there.
  • Create your user, let it finish, reboot and remove the ISO when prompted.
DISTROS.note: Erase-disk warning: on a real PC, "Erase disk" wipes the whole drive — back up first. Choose "Install alongside" or manual partitioning only if you intend to dual-boot.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

DISTROS.name: LMDE
DISTROS.best: The full Linux Mint Cinnamon experience built directly on Debian 13 instead of Ubuntu, for Mint fans who prefer Debian's base, and Mint's own fallback if Ubuntu ever disappeared. Same Mint tools, same feel, different foundation.
DISTROS.specs: ISO: 64-bit Cinnamon edition · VM: 4 GB RAM, 20 GB disk
DISTROS.watch: LMDE tracks Debian's package base, so some Ubuntu-only software and PPAs will not work here. Check for a Debian build or a Flatpak before assuming an app carries over.
DISTROS.steps:
• Boot the ISO into the live session (live user "mint", no password) and double-click Install on the desktop.
  • Language and keyboard, then choose the disk layout. In a VM, erasing the virtual disk is safe.
  • Create your user, let it finish, reboot and remove the ISO when prompted.
DISTROS.note: Erase-disk warning: on a real PC, erasing the disk wipes the whole drive — back up first. Shrink Windows from the live session first if you plan to dual-boot.
DISTROS.upd: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

GUIDES.title: What Linux is actually used for
GUIDES.excerpt: Not a hobbyist toy: Linux runs most of the web, every Android phone, and the toolkit of every security professional. Concretely, job by job.
GUIDES.body:
"Should I learn Linux?" is easier to answer when you stop asking what Linux is and ask what it does all day. The list is not abstract. Linux quietly holds up most of the computing you already use — you have just never been introduced.

Servers and the cloud

The largest job by far. The overwhelming majority of web servers, cloud instances and containers run Linux, because it is free, scriptable, stable for years at a time, and happy with no screen attached at all. If you deploy a website or an API, you are deploying it onto Linux — knowing the system your code lives on stops being optional the first time something breaks at 2 a.m.

Phones, routers, and everything embedded

Android is built on the Linux kernel, so the most common computer on Earth already runs it. So do most home routers, smart TVs, NAS boxes, industrial controllers and a good share of cars and spacecraft. Linux scales down as gracefully as it scales up.

Security and penetration testing

The security industry's tools — scanners, proxies, password auditors, network analysers — are written for Linux first, because the system's openness lets them inspect everything. Entire distributions (Kali is the famous one, see the distro cards below) exist just to bundle those tools. If your goal is cybersecurity work, Linux is not a preference; it is the workplace.

Development

Developers live where their software runs. Since production is Linux, development environments match it: containers package Linux, CI pipelines run Linux, and the terminal skills transfer unchanged from a laptop VM to a cloud server on another continent.

Privacy and old hardware

No forced account, no advertising ID, no telemetry you did not agree to — and a lightweight distro can make a ten-year-old laptop genuinely useful again instead of e-waste. For a lot of people worldwide, that last one is not a philosophy. It is the computer they can afford to keep.

Learn Linux and you are not learning an operating system. You are learning how computers actually work underneath the glass — and that knowledge transfers to every machine you will ever touch.

GUIDES.title: Install ANY Linux distro in VirtualBox
GUIDES.excerpt: One universal flow works for Ubuntu, Debian, Kali, Fedora and nearly everything else: ISO in, virtual machine built, Guest Additions, snapshot. Your real files are never at risk.
GUIDES.body:
Every distro has its own installer with its own personality, but the VirtualBox part — the part beginners fear — is identical for all of them. Learn this flow once and you can try any Linux distribution this weekend, safely, without touching your real system. The distro cards below plug into these exact steps.

1. Download VirtualBox and the ISO

Install VirtualBox from virtualbox.org (free, Windows/Mac/Linux hosts). Then download your distro's ISO — the install image, usually 1–6 GB — from the distro's official site only. An ISO is a disk in a file: VirtualBox will pretend it is a DVD in a drive.

2. Create the virtual machine

In VirtualBox: New. Give it a name ("Ubuntu test"), set Type to Linux and Version to the closest match for your distro (for example "Ubuntu (64-bit)" or "Debian (64-bit)"). Getting the version roughly right matters — it tunes defaults like the disk controller.

3. Size the RAM and CPU

Rule of thumb: never give the VM more than half your real RAM. 4 GB is a comfortable default for desktop distros (2 GB works for light ones; Kali prefers 4). Give it 2 CPU cores if your machine has 4 or more. The VM only uses this while it runs.

4. Create the virtual disk

Choose "Create a virtual hard disk now", type VDI, and — the important one — Dynamically allocated. Size: 25 GB is a safe default (30–40 for Kali with its toolset). Dynamic allocation means the file starts small and grows only as the VM actually stores data, so "25 GB" is a ceiling, not a chunk carved out of your drive today.

The safety factThat virtual disk is a single ordinary file on your computer (something like Ubuntu.vdi). The Linux inside can format it, encrypt it, destroy it — your real Windows files, photos and documents are not in that file and cannot be touched. This is the entire reason VMs are the right way to learn.

5. Attach the ISO

Select your VM → Settings → Storage → click the empty optical drive → "Choose a disk file" → pick the ISO you downloaded. The VM now believes a Linux DVD is inserted.

6. Boot and install

Start the VM. It boots from the ISO into a live session or installer. The flow is always some version of: language → keyboard → "Install" → time zone → your name and password. When it asks about the disk and offers "Erase disk and install", say yes without fear — the "disk" is your virtual file from step 4, nothing else. This is the moment the VM design earns its keep.

7. Reboot and remove the ISO

When the installer finishes it asks to restart and remove the installation medium. VirtualBox usually ejects the ISO for you; if the VM boots back into the installer, shut it down, remove the ISO in Settings → Storage, and start again — you will boot into your fresh Linux.

8. Install Guest Additions

This is the step that turns a clunky VM into a pleasant one: automatic window resizing, shared clipboard, drag-and-drop. With the VM running: Devices → Insert Guest Additions CD image, then inside Linux open the mounted disc and run the installer (or, on Debian-family systems, install the package):

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y virtualbox-guest-utils virtualbox-guest-x11

Reboot the VM afterwards. The Sandbox has a simulated run of exactly this post-install terminal session.

9. Take a snapshot

With everything fresh and working: Machine → Take Snapshot, name it "Fresh install". A snapshot is a save point for the whole machine. Every experiment you ever do starts from here — and if one goes wrong, you restore instead of reinstalling. Snapshot first is the single habit that separates calm learners from reinstall veterans.

GUIDES.title: Set up your first security lab
GUIDES.excerpt: A legal, breakable playground: Kali in VirtualBox, the network modes explained without the danger, snapshots before experiments, and the first five commands worth typing.
GUIDES.body:
Security skills are learned by breaking things, and breaking things needs a place where it is legal, safe, and reversible. That place is a lab: virtual machines on your own computer, deliberately isolated, snapshotted before every experiment. Here is the beginner build — one afternoon, no extra hardware.

The machine: Kali in VirtualBox

Install Kali Linux using the universal VirtualBox flow in the guide above — or skip the install entirely with Kali's official prebuilt VirtualBox image (import it, log in, change the default password). Kali arrives with the standard security toolkit preinstalled, which is its entire purpose. The moment it boots cleanly, take a snapshot named "Clean Kali". Every experiment starts by restoring to a known-good machine.

Network modes, explained safely

This setting decides who your VM can talk to, and it is the one place beginners can genuinely cause trouble. Three modes matter:

  • NAT (the default) — the VM can reach the internet through your host, but nothing on the internet or your home network can reach in. Safe default for updates and general use. Start here.
  • Host-only — the VM can talk to your host and your other VMs, and nothing else. No internet at all. This is the mode for attack-and-defend practice between your own machines.
  • Bridged — the VM joins your real network like another computer, with its own address, visible to everything else on it. Tools run in this mode can touch real devices. Avoid it until you can explain exactly why you need it.

Rule of the lab: if you are not sure which mode you are in, you are not ready to run the tool. NAT or Host-only, always, while learning.

Your first five commands

whoami
Who the terminal thinks you are. In Kali this answers kali — an ordinary user, despite the legends.kali@kali:~$ whoami
ip a
Your network addresses. Find the VM's own IP (often 10.0.2.15 under NAT) — you cannot practise networking without knowing where you live.kali@kali:~$ ip a
ping
The simplest "is anything there?" test there is. Three pings to a public DNS address prove your NAT networking works.kali@kali:~$ ping -c 3 1.1.1.1
sudo apt update
Refreshes the package lists so installs and upgrades offer current versions. Your first real use of sudo — one command, run as root, on purpose.kali@kali:~$ sudo apt update
nmap --version
Checks the famous scanner is installed and shows its version. Run it on day one just to prove the toolkit is real — scanning comes later, in scope, in the lab.kali@kali:~$ nmap --version

Lab rules

  • Snapshot before every experiment; restore without sentimentality when one goes sideways.
  • NAT or Host-only networking only. Bridged stays off.
  • Scan and test only machines inside this lab, or systems you have written permission to test.
  • Keep a notes file: command, what you expected, what actually happened. That file becomes your real textbook.

GUIDES.title: Linux terminal: the 15 commands that do 90% of the work
GUIDES.excerpt: There are thousands of commands. Working in the terminal daily uses a small cast of them, over and over. Learn these fifteen and the terminal stops being a wall of text.
GUIDES.body:
The terminal looks infinite from outside. From inside, a working day is the same handful of commands in rotation: look around, go somewhere, move files, read files, search files, install things. Here is that handful — the fifteen that genuinely do about ninety percent of the work — each with the one example worth memorising.

ls
List what is in the current folder. Add -la to include hidden files and details.$ ls -la
cd / pwd
cd changes folder; pwd prints where you are standing when you get lost. Everyone gets lost.$ cd ~/Downloads  ·  $ pwd
mkdir
Make a folder. The first thing you will do in every project, forever.$ mkdir projects
cp
Copy a file. Add -r for a whole folder.$ cp notes.txt notes-backup.txt
mv
Move a file — and, if the destination is the same folder with a new name, rename it.$ mv draft.txt final.txt
rm
Delete. Permanently — there is no recycle bin here, and rm -rf deletes folders and everything inside them without asking. The danger command: read the line twice before pressing Enter, every time.$ rm old-file.txt
cat
Print a whole file to the screen. Perfect for short files: configs, notes, readmes.$ cat .env.example
less
Read a long file a page at a time, with searching inside (/word) and q to quit.$ less /var/log/syslog
grep
Search inside text. The single most-used debugging command in existence: find every line that mentions a word.$ grep "error" app.log
find
Locate files by name anywhere under a folder. Your lost-file rescue service.$ find ~ -name "*.iso"
chmod
Change who may read, write or run a file. At concept level: owner / group / everyone, each with r-w-x permissions. The +x form makes a script runnable.$ chmod +x setup.sh
sudo
Run one command as root, the system boss. Honest framing: sudo is not a magic prefix for fixing errors — it removes the guardrails for that one command, so the command had better deserve it.$ sudo apt update
apt
The Debian-family software store, in text form: update refreshes the catalogue; install does what it says. (Fedora uses dnf, Arch uses pacman — same idea.)$ sudo apt install nmap
man
The manual. Every command ships its own documentation, offline, written by the people who built it. Try man before any search engine.$ man grep
history
Everything you have run, numbered. Combine with grep to answer "what was that command from Tuesday?"$ history | grep ssh

Fifteen commands, honestly learned — typed by hand, not pasted — will carry you through almost any tutorial, server, or security lab on this site. The other thousands are specialists. These are the residents.

EXPLAIN.title: Linux is a kernel, not an operating system
EXPLAIN.excerpt: The single fact that makes everything else about Linux make sense: what the kernel is, what a distribution adds on top of it, and why you never actually 'install Linux' — you install a distro.
EXPLAIN.body:
Strictly speaking, Linux is a kernel — one program, written mostly in C, first released by Linus Torvalds in 1991. The kernel is the layer that talks directly to the hardware: it schedules processes on the CPU, manages memory, reads and writes files, drives the network card, and enforces who is allowed to touch what. Everything else on a computer talks to the hardware through the kernel.

A kernel alone is not a computer you can use

Boot a bare kernel and you get no shell, no commands, no desktop — nothing to type into. A usable system also needs the userland: a shell and core utilities (historically the GNU tools, which is why you will see the name "GNU/Linux"), system libraries, an init system that starts services, a way to install software, and usually a desktop. Assembling all of that — choosing the pieces, configuring them, packaging them, maintaining them — is a job. The organisations that do that job are called distributions, or distros.

The engine and the car

The useful analogy: the kernel is an engine; a distro is a whole car built around it. Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora and Arch all run the Linux kernel — different versions, different patches — but the shell, installer, package manager, defaults and desktop wrapped around it are each distro's own choices. Two cars with the same engine can drive completely differently.

Why this matters in practice

  • "Install Linux" always means "install a distro." There is no single Linux download. The Distro Library below is a list of the cars, not the engines.
  • Skills transfer between distros because the kernel and the core commands are shared. A command learned on Ubuntu works on a Debian server and mostly on Arch, because underneath, it is the same system.
  • Android runs the Linux kernel too — with a completely different userland on top. Same engine, unrecognisable car. That is how far the kernel/distro distinction stretches.
  • When something is "a Linux problem," ask which layer. A wifi driver is kernel territory; a missing app is the distro's package catalogue; a ugly desktop is the desktop environment, which most distros let you swap.

The pieces every distro assembles

  • Kernel — which version, how often it updates, which drivers are built in.
  • Init system — starts and supervises services. Most distros use systemd; a few (Devuan, Artix, Void) exist specifically to offer something else.
  • Package manager — how software is installed and updated: APT, DNF, Pacman, Zypper and friends. This is the difference you will feel daily.
  • Desktop environment — GNOME, KDE Plasma, Xfce, Cinnamon and others: the look, the weight, the workflow.
  • Release model and defaults — fixed versions vs rolling updates, and what is preinstalled, which the next articles take apart.

So you never choose "Linux." You choose a distro — a particular assembly of shared parts, with a particular temperament. Choosing well is mostly about matching that temperament to the job, which is exactly what the rest of this section is for.

EXPLAIN.title: How distros actually differ
EXPLAIN.excerpt: Strip away the logos and most distros share the same kernel, commands and apps. The real differences are five: package manager, release model, desktop, defaults and community — and only some of them matter day to day.
EXPLAIN.body:
There are hundreds of Linux distributions, and the internet argues about them as if they were different species. They are not. Almost all of them ship the same kernel lineage, the same core commands, the same browsers and office suites. What genuinely differs fits on one hand — and knowing the list stops distro choice from feeling like a personality test.

1. The package manager — the difference you feel daily

Software on Linux comes from your distro's repositories, installed with its package manager. Debian-family systems use APT with .deb packages; Fedora and the Red Hat family use DNF with .rpm; Arch uses Pacman; openSUSE uses Zypper. The commands differ (apt install vs pacman -S) but the idea is identical — and the repo's size and freshness shape your whole experience. This is also what "family" means in the library below: distros in a family share this machinery and most of their tutorials.

2. The release model — how updates arrive

Fixed releases ship a tested version, then maintain it with security fixes for years (Ubuntu LTS, Debian, Leap). Rolling releases update continuously with no versions at all (Arch, Tumbleweed). Neither is "better" — they trade newness against stillness. The next article gives this the space it deserves.

3. The desktop environment — the difference you see

GNOME is minimal and keyboard-friendly; KDE Plasma is configurable to the pixel; Xfce and LXQt are light enough for decade-old hardware; Cinnamon feels like classic Windows. Crucially, the desktop is a layer, not the distro: most distros offer several editions or let you install another desktop later. People switch distros over desktops they could have changed in an afternoon.

4. Defaults and philosophy

What is preinstalled, whether proprietary drivers and media codecs are one click or a deliberate errand (Fedora makes it an errand; Mint does not), whether anything phones home (mainstream Linux distros collect no telemetry by default — a real difference from Windows), and how the project is governed: volunteer community (Debian, Arch), company-backed (Ubuntu/Canonical, Fedora/Red Hat), or one person's spare time. Governance decides how much you should bet on a distro still existing in five years.

5. Community and documentation

When something breaks at midnight, your distro's community is your support department. Ubuntu has the largest crowd and the most answered questions; Arch has the Arch Wiki, the best technical documentation in the Linux world, readable and useful even if you never run Arch. Small distros can be excellent and still leave you alone with a rare error message.

What barely differs

The terminal's core commands, the filesystem layout, the permissions model, SSH, scripting, and the catalogue of serious applications — Firefox, LibreOffice, VLC, GIMP, VS Code and friends exist everywhere. Flatpak has narrowed even the package gap, offering the same app builds on any distro. Choose on the five real axes; everything else follows you from distro to distro.

EXPLAIN.title: Rolling vs fixed releases: how your system ages
EXPLAIN.excerpt: The deepest split between distros is not the desktop or the logo — it is whether your system stands still and gets patched, or flows forward forever. Honest pros, cons, and the sensible middle grounds.
EXPLAIN.body:
Every distro answers one question differently: after you install it, what happens next? Fixed releases answer "as little as possible, for years." Rolling releases answer "everything, continuously." Your tolerance for surprises should make this choice, not fashion.

Fixed (point) releases

The distro publishes a version — tested as a whole — then freezes its software and backports only security and bug fixes. Debian Stable, Ubuntu LTS (a new long-term release every two years, supported for five), Linux Mint and openSUSE Leap work this way. Upgrading to the next version is a deliberate event, an hour with a progress bar, a few times a decade.

  • Pros: the system behaves the same on day 400 as day 1; tutorials stay accurate; ideal for servers and for people who think about their OS never.
  • Cons: applications age. Your browser and tools may be a version or two behind — narrowed a lot by Flatpak and vendor downloads, but real.

Rolling releases

No versions: packages land as their developers release them, and your system is simply "current." Arch, Manjaro (which holds Arch's packages back briefly for extra testing), EndeavourOS, Garuda, openSUSE Tumbleweed and Solus live here. You never do a big version upgrade; you also never stop upgrading.

  • Pros: the newest kernel, drivers and apps — new hardware support arrives first here, and gamers chasing the latest graphics stack benefit.
  • Cons: occasionally an update changes behaviour or breaks something, and the fix is yours to apply. The mature answer is snapshots: Tumbleweed configures Snapper automatically, so a bad update is a reboot into yesterday. Rolling without snapshots is bravado; rolling with them is a system.

The middle grounds

Fedora releases roughly every six months with fresh packages — fixed in name, brisk in practice. Ubuntu's ordinary (non-LTS) releases do the same on a six-month beat. These suit people who want current software but prefer their change in scheduled doses.

The honest rule

Servers, work machines you cannot afford to fiddle with, and first installs: fixed LTS. You will forget the system exists, which is the highest praise an OS earns. Enthusiasts, new hardware, and anyone who enjoys the platform itself: rolling, with snapshots on. And never let anyone shame you either way — the person who never thinks about updates and the person who reads them for fun are both using Linux correctly.

EXPLAIN.title: Which distro for which job
EXPLAIN.excerpt: Beginner, gaming, servers, security work, old laptops, privacy — the honest shortlist for each job, drawn from the library below, including the cases where the famous answer is the wrong one.
EXPLAIN.body:
Distro arguments usually start from loyalty. Start from the job instead. Here is the shortlist this library's guides back up — with the reasoning, and the traps.

Your first distro

Linux Mint if you are coming from Windows and want your habits respected; Ubuntu if you want the largest community and the most tutorials written for your exact system. Zorin OS earns a mention for making Windows and macOS switchers feel at home with switchable layouts. The trap: starting on Arch or Gentoo "to learn properly." You will learn — mostly that you wanted a working computer. Walk first; the manual distros keep.

Gaming

Nobara (a Fedora remix by the author of Proton-GE, with drivers, codecs and game fixes pre-applied) and Bazzite (an image-based Fedora built to feel like a Steam Deck for any PC) exist precisely so you skip a weekend of setup. Pop!_OS with its separate NVIDIA ISO is the polished general-purpose option. Honest footnote: with Steam and Proton, most mainstream distros game well now — these three just remove the errands.

Servers

Debian for calm, community-run stability; Ubuntu Server for the biggest ecosystem of guides; Rocky Linux or AlmaLinux when the job wants Red Hat Enterprise Linux compatibility without the subscription; CentOS Stream if you deliberately want to live slightly ahead of RHEL. Fixed releases, all of them — servers should be boring.

Security work

Kali Linux or Parrot OS — run in VirtualBox, under the lab rules in this section's security-lab guide. The trap: installing Kali as your only, daily system. It is a toolbox, not a home; do your banking elsewhere.

Old laptops and weak hardware

MX Linux, antiX, Linux Lite and the light Ubuntu flavours (Lubuntu, Xubuntu) genuinely revive machines Windows has abandoned. Honest mechanics: it is the desktop (Xfce, LXQt, IceWM) that does most of the saving, not the badge — and an inexpensive SSD upgrade beats any distro choice. Below about 2 GB of RAM, antiX is the realistic floor.

Privacy

Baseline first: every mainstream distro here is private next to Windows — no account requirement, no advertising ID, no default telemetry. Beyond that: Tails for amnesic, leave-no-trace sessions from a USB stick (journalists, travel, shared machines) and Qubes OS for a daily system built from isolated compartments, if your hardware and patience qualify. The trap: believing a distro alone makes you anonymous — your browser habits matter more than your boot screen.

Learning how Linux really works

Debian or Ubuntu until the terminal feels like furniture, then Arch (with the Arch Wiki as your textbook) and, when you want the final boss, Gentoo, where you compile the system yourself. In a VM, with snapshots, at your own pace.

The closing honesty: the distance between the "best" and "worst" mainstream distro for any job is smaller than a month of actually using one. Pick from the shortlist, install it the safe way below, and start. You can always move — your files and skills come with you.
